topic: Day 2 · Stroke in Special Populations & the Mimics
speakerBio: Specialises in young and unusual stroke and the art of not thrombolysing a mimic.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 34-year-old with no vascular risk factors has a stroke. The reflex work-up will be normal — because you are looking in the wrong place. Young stroke, pregnancy-related stroke and cerebral venous thrombosis follow different rules, and the mimics can fool you into thrombolysing a brain that never had a clot. This session is about not being caught out.

1 · Young stroke — a different differential

In the young, "atherosclerosis" is rarely the answer — think dissection, a hole in the heart, inflamed or clotting blood, and drugs.
CauseClue / test
Cervical artery dissectionNeck pain, Horner's, trauma/manipulation — CTA/MRA
PFO / paradoxical embolismBubble echo (TOE), leg/pelvic DVT, Valsalva onset
Vasculitis / CNS inflammationSystemic features, raised inflammatory markers, vessel imaging
Thrombophilia / antiphospholipidRecurrent clots, miscarriages, prolonged APTT — warfarin for APS
Illicit drugs (cocaine, amphetamines)History, toxicology
Genetic (CADASIL, Fabry, MELAS)Family history, migraine, white-matter pattern

2 · Stroke in pregnancy & the puerperium

Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable, high-risk window. Consider pre-eclampsia/eclampsia and PRES (posterior reversible encephalopathy — headache, seizures, visual loss, occipital oedema), cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (below), and standard ischaemic/haemorrhagic strokes. Reperfusion decisions are individualised with obstetrics; do not withhold work-up because a patient is pregnant.

3 · Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST)

💡 The stroke that breaks the arterial rules

CVST presents with headache (often progressive), seizures, and focal signs, sometimes with papilloedema. Venous infarcts cross arterial territories, are frequently haemorrhagic, and favour risk factors like pregnancy/puerperium, the oral contraceptive pill, dehydration and thrombophilia. Diagnose with CT/MR venography. The counter-intuitive treatment: anticoagulate — even in the presence of venous haemorrhage — because stopping clot propagation improves outcome.

4 · The mimics — don't lyse a non-stroke

  • Hypoglycaemia (check glucose always), seizure with Todd's paresis, migraine with aura (positive, spreading symptoms), functional deficits, MS/demyelination, tumour, and encephalitis.
  • The safeguards: a clear onset history, the pattern of symptoms, a glucose, and urgent imaging — thrombolysing a mimic is usually low-yield and occasionally harmful, while missing a real stroke costs brain.
☠️ M&M — the missed CVST

A young woman on the combined pill with a week of worsening headache then a seizure was treated for "migraine and a first fit"; her CT showed a small "haemorrhage" that was actually a venous infarct. The diagnosis of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis was made only after she deteriorated. Lesson: progressive headache + seizure + focal signs (especially with a prothrombotic risk factor, or a haemorrhage that crosses arterial territories) should trigger a venogram — and CVST is anticoagulated even when it has bled.

5 · Take-home

  • Young stroke: hunt dissection, PFO, vasculitis, thrombophilia/APS, drugs, genetics — not atherosclerosis.
  • Pregnancy: think pre-eclampsia/PRES and CVST; still investigate fully.
  • CVST — headache + seizure + haemorrhagic cross-territory infarct; diagnose with venography, anticoagulate even if haemorrhagic.
  • Respect the mimics: glucose, history and imaging keep you from lysing a non-stroke.

moderatorQs.q: How is the work-up different in a young stroke?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: You abandon the atherosclerosis reflex and hunt a different list: cervical artery dissection (neck pain, Horner's), PFO/paradoxical embolism (bubble echo, leg/pelvic DVT), vasculitis, thrombophilia and antiphospholipid syndrome (which is anticoagulated with warfarin), illicit drugs, and genetic causes like CADASIL or Fabry. The history — trauma, migraine, family history, drug use — usually points the way.

moderatorQs.q: Why does cerebral venous sinus thrombosis break the usual rules?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because it is venous. It presents with progressive headache, seizures and focal signs, its infarcts cross arterial territories and are often haemorrhagic, and it favours prothrombotic states (pregnancy/puerperium, the oral contraceptive pill, dehydration, thrombophilia). It is diagnosed on CT/MR venography, and — counter-intuitively — it is anticoagulated even when it has bled, because stopping clot propagation improves outcome.

moderatorQs.q: How do you avoid thrombolysing a mimic while not missing a real stroke?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Check a glucose every time, take a precise onset and symptom history (positive/spreading vs negative deficits, stereotypy), and image urgently. Migraine aura, seizure with Todd's paresis, hypoglycaemia and functional presentations are the common mimics; the CT and the clinical pattern together protect you at both ends — thrombolysing a mimic is usually low-yield, while missing a real stroke costs brain.

audienceQs.q: Young woman on the pill with a week of worsening headache and a seizure — what next?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Think cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Progressive headache plus seizure plus focal signs — especially with a prothrombotic risk factor, or a haemorrhage that crosses arterial territories — should trigger a CT/MR venogram. If confirmed, anticoagulate even in the presence of venous haemorrhage.

audienceQs.q: Which thrombophilia should I not miss because it changes treatment?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Antiphospholipid syndrome — suspect it with unprovoked venous and arterial clots, recurrent miscarriage, or an unexplained prolonged APTT, and confirm the antibodies. It matters because high-risk APS is anticoagulated with warfarin, not a DOAC (which increased arterial events in triple-positive patients), so getting the diagnosis changes the drug.
